questions.prompt: Where does GitHub look for workflow files?
choices: .github/workflows/
.github/
workflows/ at the repository root
Anywhere, as long as the file ends in .yml
questions.explain: Workflows are read from .github/workflows/. The file name itself does not matter.

questions.prompt: Two jobs in the same workflow need the same built files. What has to happen?
choices: Nothing, jobs share a working directory
The files must be passed between them, because each job gets its own runner
The second job must use the same runs-on label
They must be in the same workflow file
questions.explain: Every job starts on a fresh machine. Sharing files between jobs takes a deliberate step, such as an artifact.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a step's uses and run?
choices: uses runs a command, run calls an action
uses calls a reusable action, run executes a shell command
They are the same, but run is older
uses only works in the first step of a job
questions.explain: uses calls an action someone published; run executes the command you write, in the job's shell.

questions.prompt: Why do most jobs start with actions/checkout?
choices: It installs Node
It logs in to GitHub
The runner starts without your code, so the job has to fetch it
It is required before any run step
questions.explain: A runner begins as an empty machine. Checkout is what puts your repository on it.

choices: A reusable step published by someone else
The machine that executes a job
The event that starts a workflow
A container image for your application
questions.explain: A runner is the machine a job runs on, hosted by GitHub or by you.

questions.prompt: A build that changed nothing breaks overnight. Why is the runner image a suspect?
choices: Images are rebuilt regularly, so the preinstalled software can move under you
Runners lose their cache each night
GitHub restarts runners daily
Images are chosen at random
questions.explain: Hosted images are updated regularly. The run log records which image it used, under Set up job.

questions.prompt: Which kind of action only runs on Linux runners?
choices: JavaScript
Composite
Docker container
All of them run everywhere
questions.explain: Docker container actions require a Linux runner, and are slower to start because the container must be built or pulled.

questions.prompt: Why does GitHub suggest using an action rather than a bare command for tool setup?
choices: Actions are always faster
An action lets you choose a version, so the tool stays the same regardless of image updates
Commands are not allowed in public repositories
Actions skip the runner
questions.explain: Version selection is the point: it pins what you use instead of whatever the image ships this week.

choices: .github/workflow/ci.yml
.github/workflows/anything.yml
workflows/ci.yaml at the repository root
.github/ci.yml
questions.explain: Any .yml or .yaml file directly inside .github/workflows/ is a workflow, whatever it is called.

questions.prompt: You fix a broken workflow on a branch. Where does the fix take effect?
choices: Everywhere immediately
On the branch that has the fix, because the version that runs is the one on the triggering branch
Only after merging to the default branch
Only after the next scheduled run
questions.explain: A workflow file is part of the branch. Some events, such as schedules, are the exception and use the default branch.

questions.prompt: Why split work across several workflow files?
choices: GitHub limits a file to one job
Each file has its own triggers, so unrelated work does not re-run
Smaller files run faster
Only one file can use secrets
questions.explain: Files are the unit people read and disable, and separate triggers keep a deployment change from re-running the tests.

questions.prompt: What happens if you indent a workflow file with tab characters?
choices: Nothing, tabs and spaces are equivalent
The file fails to parse, because YAML does not allow tabs for indentation
The tabs are converted to two spaces
Only the affected job is skipped
questions.explain: A tab is a syntax error in YAML. Use spaces, conventionally two per level.

questions.prompt: You write python-version: 3.10 without quotes. What does the parser see?
choices: The text 3.10
The number 3.1
An error
The number 310
questions.explain: It is read as a number, and the trailing zero is lost. Quote versions so they stay text.

questions.prompt: Why do some projects write "on": with quotes?
choices: GitHub requires it
Older YAML reads bare on as a boolean, and some tools that read the file still do
It makes the workflow run sooner
It is needed for scheduled workflows
questions.explain: GitHub's parser reads the key as text, but linters and other tools reading YAML 1.1 may not, so the quotes remove all doubt.

questions.prompt: Which is true of flow style, as in branches: [main, 'releases/**']?
choices: It is not valid in workflows
It means something different from the block list
It means the same, but patterns containing brackets must be quoted
It only works for branches
questions.explain: Both styles express the same list. In flow style a pattern with [ or ] has to be quoted to parse.
